video.title: Shoulder Adduction Unlocks the Tennis Forehand

classification.reason: The coach explains the mechanics of shoulder adduction as the final link in the forehand, demonstrates how to establish a consistent contact zone, and shows posture adjustments for varied ball positions.

problem.title_as_question: How should shoulder adduction be harnessed in the forehand to create a consistent contact zone?
problem.definition: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls across the body and turns the hand inward, which can send the ball sideways or downward unless the player positions the body and contact zone so that the pull drives back to front toward the target.
prerequisites: Basic forehand grip and swing motion
problem.target_player: Players from 2.5 to 4.5 who want to stop framing and missing consistently

symptoms.description: The ball is struck sideways and downwards into the net or off court.
The ball shanks or frames off the outside edge of the racket.
The racket face closes excessively through the contact zone, rotating up to 100 degrees.
The hitting elbow remains trapped behind the plane of the hips during the forward swing.

causes.statement: The player executes shoulder adduction without orienting the swing so the cross-body pull drives back to front toward the target.
The player allows active or excessive internal shoulder rotation, drastically rolling the racket face over through contact.
The hitting elbow fails to travel past the plane of the hips before shoulder adduction is engaged.
The player fails to probe and position the body relative to the ball to place it in the usable shoulder adduction window.
The hitting shoulder does not rotate forward in front of the non-hitting shoulder on standard groundstrokes.
The player attempts to generate speed via torso uncoiling before establishing spatial awareness and feel for the final arm link.

angles.summary: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls across the torso and internally rotates the arm, requiring the elbow to pass the hip plane so that cross-body pulling acts back-to-front toward the target.
Players should isolate and feel what it is like to swing through contact with a stable string angle that changes by only around 10 degrees.
Players believe clean contact requires engaging the full kinetic chain and torso rotation, but clean ball striking only requires mastering the final arm link.
Professional players dealing with bad bounces adapt their swing path to still utilize shoulder adduction without shanking.
On low balls, tilting the hips preserves the proper arm-to-torso alignment for shoulder adduction rather than simply dropping the arm downward.

solutions.summary: Verify that the hitting elbow travels forward past the plane of the hips before initiating shoulder adduction through the ball.
solutions.external_goal: The hitting elbow moves past the plane of the hips toward the net.

solutions.summary: Check that the racket face is set on a slight downward angle and changes by no more than about 10 degrees across the contact zone rather than completely closing.
solutions.external_goal: Racket strings maintain a slight downward angle across the contact zone.

solutions.summary: Perform comfortable shadow swings focusing solely on the final arm motion to build the feeling of adduction driving back to front into a designated contact zone.
Pull across your body rather than pushing forward so that the natural adduction trajectory aligns straight through toward the target.
Practice adjusting body tilt for varied ball heights (e.g., tilting hips on low balls) so the shoulder adduction movement consistently hits back to front.
solutions.external_goal: Tilt hips to align the torso and arm in the standard contact orientation relative to the incoming ball height.
